# Theory

## Class-Based Segregation and Homophily

US society is strongly segregated based on class, in terms of both income and educational attainment [@mijs2021]. Analysis of General Social Survey data indicates that an increasing difference in the number of years of education received negatively affected the probability of naming someone as a core confidant, and that this association has even become somewhat stronger between 1985 and 2004 [@smith2014]. This is likely to extend to college communities. Studies on the experiences of first-generation college students highlight that classism [@allan2016], microaggressions [@gray2017; @álvarez-rivadulla2023], and insensitivity [@salusky2022] create barriers to forming and maintaining cross-class friendships. On a micro level, this suggests the following hypothesis:

*H1: Students prefer maintaining friendships with peers who have the same parental educational background.*

On a macro level, homophily suggests that the college social network will be segregated along students' parental educational backgrounds:

*H2: Students who hang out together are more similar with regards to parental educational backgrounds than students who do not hang out together.*

## Family Socialisation

Importantly however, social distance between different group categories is not fixed. As evidenced by the observed tendency for homophily on specific categories to fluctuate over time [@smith2014], it is a context-dependent measure. Just as context may change over time on a national level, it may differ between communities or personal networks. This study therefore considers class categorisation to be a *social construct*, and its relevance for behaviour as something that is *socially learnt*.

An important share of social learning happens within families.

Cross-class embeddedness!

*H3: Students whose parents have different educational backgrounds ("mixed background") will demonstrate lower levels of homophily in friendship maintenance than students whose parents have the attained the same level of education.*
